passage: I still remember the exact second it left my mouth. We were on the school bus, everyone was guessing who liked whom, and I was so excited to have real news that I said, "Parul is nervous about the singing audition. She might not go." She had told me not to tell anyone. Within an hour half of class ten knew. Next day Parul walked past me with her jaw set. At lunch I hid behind my book and rehearsed excuses: everyone already knew, you should have said it was serious. None of them sounded true. At the gate I caught her and said, "I told them. It was my fault. I was excited and I didn't think. I'm sorry." She said she was angry and didn't want to talk yet. I said okay and let her go. It stung, but it was fair. — Vasudha

qa.q: Where were Vasudha and the others when Vasudha said Parul's secret?
qa.a: They were on the school bus.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha stop rehearsing excuses?
qa.a: Vasudha was ashamed and could not face Parul, and none of the excuses sounded true, so Vasudha chose a plain apology instead.

qa.q: What made Vasudha's apology a wise one?
qa.a: Vasudha said "It was my fault" with no excuse, accepted that Parul was angry, and let her have distance.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt at the gate?
qa.a: Angry and hurt. Her jaw set earlier and her words that she did not want to talk yet suggest she needs space, and it may take time.

grounding: Vasudha leaked a friend's secret from excitement, cannot face her, and apologises plainly and gives distance.

passage:
Tuesday. Dilnaz told Thomas at the bus stop: she'd been selected for the national youth orchestra. "Don't tell anyone yet. Not till it's official."
Thursday. In the library, Thomas was so excited he blurted it to four people. "Dilnaz is going national! Can you believe it?" By lunch it was all over school. By evening Dilnaz had heard.
Friday. She didn't sit near him on the bus. Thomas couldn't look at her. He kept rehearsing excuses: I was proud of you, it slipped out, it's good news anyway.
Monday. He found her outside the music room. "I told people. I shouldn't have. I'm sorry." No excuse.
Dilnaz glared. "You made my moment yours."
"You're right." He stood there and took it.
"I don't want to talk for a while."
"Okay," he said, and walked away. It was the hardest thing he'd done all week.

qa.q: Which orchestra was Dilnaz selected for?
Why couldn't Thomas look at Dilnaz on Friday?
qa.a: He felt deeply ashamed of blurting her news and was tempted to hide behind excuses.

qa.q: What made Thomas's apology on Monday a good one?
qa.a: It was plain, with no excuses, he accepted her anger and he gave her the distance she asked for.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the leak?
qa.a: She feels angry and robbed, as if Thomas took her special moment and made it his own.

grounding: A teen who leaked a friend's secret out of excitement feels ashamed, apologises plainly, accepts her anger and gives distance.

passage:
Thomas, come here. You look like someone who broke something. I know that face.
When I was fifteen, my best friend Hari's father was very sick, and Hari told only me. One afternoon, all excited because I'd been made cricket captain, I was chattering to the team and it just spilled out: "Hari can't come, his father's in the hospital." I said it like news.
Hari heard. He looked at me like I was a stranger.
I wanted to say it was an accident, that I meant well. I almost said, "You should have told me not to." That was the lie ready on my tongue.
Instead, the next morning I went to his house. I said, "I told them. I was wrong. No excuse." He shouted at me. I stood and let him.
I stayed away for a month. Then he called me.
I'm Chinmay, sixty-eight now, and he's still my oldest friend.

qa.q: How old was the speaker when this happened?
How did young Chinmay feel after Hari heard him?
qa.a: Chinmay felt ashamed and tempted to make excuses or even blame Hari, before choosing to apologise.

qa.q: Which choice in the story was the turning point?
qa.a: Chinmay went to Hari's house and admitted it plainly with no excuse, then accepted his shouting and gave him a month of space.

qa.q: What might Hari have felt when he heard his father's illness mentioned casually?
qa.a: Hari probably felt betrayed and hurt, as if something painful and private had become gossip.

grounding: An elder recalls leaking a friend's painful secret, then apologising without excuses, accepting anger and giving distance.
